overview.title: 📖 Overview: Does Sprinkling Work After the Meat Already Left?
overview.subtitle: Meilah 6a–6b
overview.hebrewSource: בְּשַׂר קׇדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים שֶׁיָּצָא לִפְנֵי זְרִיקַת דָּמִים
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara continues testing baraitot against the 'fitness of sprinkling' vs. 'fitness of eating' debate, refining two of Rabbi Shimon's teachings — on notar and on piggul — to mean 'fit for sprinkling' rather than 'actually sprinkled.' A final round of testing yields a broader principle: sprinkling that would bring an offering INTO me'ilah must be proper, while sprinkling that REMOVES an offering from me'ilah works even if performed improperly. The daf then turns to a new mishna: meat of the most sacred offerings that left the Temple courtyard before its blood was sprinkled, then came back in — do we say the sprinkling still works to protect it from me'ilah? Rabbi Eliezer says no; Rabbi Akiva says yes, bringing a striking proof from the case of two sin offerings, one lost and one designated in its place.

slides.title: 🌙 Refining Rabbi Shimon's Baraita on Notar
slides.subtitle: 'Before sprinkling' vs. 'after sprinkling' turns out to mean something more precise

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Shimon: meat eaten before the blood's sprinkling → me'ilah; after sprinkling → no me'ilah
2️⃣ Challenge: if there was still time in the day to sprinkle the collected blood, yet me'ilah still applies — doesn't that prove only ACTUAL sprinkling (not mere fitness) removes me'ilah?
3️⃣ Gemara deflects: no, the case is blood collected just before sunset, with NO time left to sprinkle that day
4️⃣ So Rabbi Shimon's real distinction is: before the blood was fit for sprinkling vs. after it became fit for sprinkling

callout.label: Same pattern repeats:
callout.text: A parallel baraita about piggul ('there is piggul subject to me'ilah and piggul that is not') is tested and refined the identical way — proving nothing new, but reinforcing that 'fit for sprinkling' is the operative standard.

slides.title: 🚫 Notar and Piggul: The Same Structure, The Same Refinement
slides.subtitle: Two baraitot, one underlying test

boxes.title: Notar Baraita
items: 'There is notar subject to me'ilah, and notar that is not'
After fit-for-sprinkling → me'ilah does not apply

boxes.title: Piggul Baraita
items: 'There is piggul subject to me'ilah, and piggul that is not'

callout.label: Why cite both?
callout.text: Each attempted proof for 'fitness of eating' is independently deflected in the same way — the Gemara shows the parallel doesn't settle the Ḥizkiya/Rabbi Yoḥanan debate either way.

slides.title: 📐 A Governing Principle Emerges
slides.subtitle: When must sprinkling be performed properly to matter?
slides.hebrewSource: כֹּל לְאֵיתוֹיֵי לִידֵי מְעִילָה, זְרִיקָה כְּתִיקְנָהּ מַיְיתֵי לִידֵי מְעִילָה. כֹּל לְאַפּוֹקֵי מִידֵי מְעִילָה, אֲפִילּוּ שֶׁלֹּא כְּתִיקְנָהּ נָמֵי מַפְּקָא
slides.label: The rule:
slides.text: Testing yet another version of 'the piggul is always subject to me'ilah,' the Gemara extracts a broader principle: wherever sprinkling's role is to bring an offering INTO me'ilah — like the sacrificial portions of offerings of lesser sanctity — only a proper sprinkling has that effect. But wherever sprinkling's role is to remove an offering FROM me'ilah — like the meat of offerings of the most sacred order — even an improper sprinkling achieves that removal. Notably, this conclusion is not in accordance with Rav Giddel's stricter rule from the previous dafim.

slides.title: 🔄 New Mishna: Meat That Left the Courtyard Before Sprinkling
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Rabbi Akiva on whether sprinkling still protects it

lines.speaker: R' Eliezer
lines.text: The sprinkling doesn't help — the meat already left before the blood was sprinkled, so it's subject to me'ilah, but exempt from piggul, notar, and tamei violations (since it never became properly permitted).

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: The sprinkling IS effective even though the meat already left — so it's exempt from me'ilah, but now DOES carry liability for piggul, notar, and tamei (since it's treated as properly permitted meat).

lines.speaker: R' Akiva's proof
lines.text: Consider: a man loses his sin offering, designates a replacement, then the first is found — both stand fit. If he sprinkles one animal's blood, that exempts the OTHER animal's meat too, since either could have been chosen.

lines.speaker: Kal vaChomer
lines.text: If sprinkling one animal's blood can exempt an entirely different animal's meat from me'ilah, all the more so it should exempt its OWN meat — even meat that left the courtyard!

callout.label: Same dispute, opposite offerings:
callout.text: For sacrificial portions of offerings of LESSER sanctity that left before sprinkling, the mishna flips the positions: Rabbi Eliezer says sprinkling is ineffective (no me'ilah, no piggul/notar/tamei), Rabbi Akiva says it IS effective (me'ilah applies, piggul/notar/tamei apply).

slides.title: ⚖️ Why the Mishna Needs Both Cases — and Rabbi Yoḥanan's Limit
slides.subtitle: Kodshei kodashim and kodashim kalim each teach something the other could not
headers: If Only This Case Were Taught...
rows: I'd think Rabbi Eliezer requires PROPER sprinkling only to remove me'ilah — but concedes improper sprinkling still ADDS me'ilah for lesser offerings
I'd think Rabbi Akiva requires only that sprinkling ADDS me'ilah even if improper — but concedes it takes PROPER sprinkling to remove me'ilah for sacred-order meat
Shows the tanna'im truly disagree on both fronts — neither concedes to the other in either direction
Rabbi Yoḥanan's qualification of R' Akiva
Sprinkling exempts meat that left ONLY if part of the offering remained inside the courtyard — if the ENTIRE offering left, Rabbi Akiva agrees sprinkling does not help

summary.principle: Sprinkling's power depends on its direction: bringing an offering into me'ilah requires a proper sprinkling, while removing an offering from me'ilah can happen even through an improper one — and Rabbi Akiva's view that sprinkling protects meat that already left the courtyard applies, per Rabbi Yoḥanan, only when part of the offering remained inside.

flowSteps.content: 🌙 Rabbi Shimon's notar/piggul baraitot refined: the real line is 'fit for sprinkling', not 'actually sprinkled'
📐 General principle: proper sprinkling needed to ADD me'ilah; even improper sprinkling can REMOVE me'ilah

columns.content: 🔄 R' Eliezer: meat that left before sprinkling stays subject to me'ilah, exempt from piggul/notar/tamei
⚖️ R' Akiva: sprinkling still works — exempt from me'ilah, but now liable for piggul/notar/tamei

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Rabbi Akiva's protective sprinkling only functions when part of the offering remained inside the courtyard (Rabbi Yoḥanan)

quiz.q: How does the Gemara refine Rabbi Shimon's statement that 'there is notar subject to me'ilah and notar that is not'?
o: The distinction is whether the animal was male or female
The real distinction is whether the blood was 'fit for sprinkling' (sunset had not yet come) or not, not whether it was actually sprinkled
The distinction is only about sin offerings
There is no valid distinction; the baraita is rejected entirely
quiz.e: After challenge and refutation, the Gemara concludes Rabbi Shimon's true distinction is between blood that had not yet become fit for sprinkling (collected just before sunset) and blood that had become fit.

quiz.q: What general principle does the Gemara extract about when sprinkling must be performed properly to have an effect on me'ilah?
o: Sprinkling always needs to be proper, no exceptions
Proper sprinkling is required to bring an offering INTO me'ilah, but even improper sprinkling can REMOVE an offering from me'ilah
Sprinkling never affects me'ilah status
Only the time of day sprinkling occurs matters, not its validity
quiz.e: The Gemara concludes that where sprinkling's role is to add an offering to the category of me'ilah, it must be proper; where its role is to remove an offering from me'ilah, even an improper sprinkling suffices.

quiz.q: In the new mishna, what do Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva disagree about regarding meat of the most sacred offerings that left the courtyard before the blood was sprinkled?
o: Whether the meat may be eaten by non-priests
Whether the sprinkling, performed after the meat already left, is effective to remove the meat from me'ilah and subject it to piggul/notar/tamei liability instead
Whether the blood itself may be sprinkled at all
Whether the animal needs to be slaughtered again
quiz.e: Rabbi Eliezer holds the sprinkling is ineffective for meat that already left (still me'ilah, no piggul/notar/tamei); Rabbi Akiva holds it is effective (no me'ilah, but piggul/notar/tamei apply).

quiz.q: What proof does Rabbi Akiva bring from the case of a lost sin offering and its replacement?
o: That two sin offerings can never be sacrificed together
That sprinkling one animal's blood exempts even the OTHER animal's meat from me'ilah, so a fortiori it should exempt its own meat that merely left the courtyard
That lost animals are always disqualified
That sin offerings are never subject to me'ilah
quiz.e: Since sprinkling one animal's blood can exempt a completely different animal's meat (because either could have been chosen), Rabbi Akiva argues by kal vaḥomer that it certainly exempts its own meat, even meat that left the courtyard.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, when does Rabbi Akiva agree that sprinkling is effective to remove meat that left the courtyard from me'ilah?
o: Only when the entire offering left the courtyard
Only when part of the offering left the courtyard while part remained inside
Never — Rabbi Yoḥanan says Rabbi Akiva always requires the meat to stay inside
Only for offerings of lesser sanctity
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan limits Rabbi Akiva's ruling to a case where only part of the offering left the courtyard; if the entire offering left, Rabbi Akiva agrees the sprinkling does not remove it from me'ilah.
